name: Emeka Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Calder Row Accountants, about thirty staff in an old mill building by the canal. I lead a team of four, and our patch is charities, community groups and co-ops, plus tax returns for the small businesses that grew out of them. A normal day is reviewing my team's files in the morning, then meeting treasurers in the afternoon, who are often retired teachers with a shoebox and a lot of goodwill.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy most, and what grinds you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the charity work, because I can see where the money goes: a food bank's freezer, a youth club's minibus. What wears me out is the pay gap. I'm chartered with a master's, I'm leading a team, and I still earn less than the people doing corporate audit upstairs, and after rent Ruth and I have almost nothing left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That feels plausible. I already use one of the chat tools now and then for drafting letters to treasurers, and it's handy, but it's not running my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool and nothing more, and I'd be glad. At work I'd tell my team we keep the same approach, just a bit quicker on the letters. Online I'd probably post something about tech bosses overselling things again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad for the jobs but it doesn't fix my real problem. We've got less than a month of savings, Ruth's teaching salary is fixed, and there are only two other firms in the city that do charity work. If Calder Row lost a big contract, I've nowhere obvious to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and use the drafting tool a bit more for the dull letters. I'd ask for the pay rise I've been putting off, and I'd set up a standing order of a hundred a month into savings, even if it hurts. I'd also want the firm to sign the fair pay pledge the charity sector keeps talking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady. There's a low hum of worry about money, but that hum was there long before AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the hum was already there. What's behind it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last winter the boiler went and we put the repair on a credit card. It took us five months to clear it. One more thing like that and we're borrowing from Ruth's parents, which I'd hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you actually ask for the rise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask, politely and with numbers, because that's what I'm good at. I'd show the partners what my team billed last year against what I'm paid. I've rehearsed it in the shower about twenty times.

say: I'd say AI is a **useful tool** and the scare was overblown by **tech bosses**.
I'd tell my team we keep our approach, just with **quicker letters**.
think: Privately, the real problem is **less than a month** of savings and a fixed household income.
Only **two other firms** in the city do charity work, so I've nowhere obvious to go.
do: Use the drafting tool more for **routine letters** to charity treasurers.
Ask for a **pay rise** with billing figures, and save **a hundred** a month.
feel: Mostly **steady**, with a low hum of **money worry** that predates AI.
S0.quote: Last winter the boiler went and we put the repair on a credit card. It took us five months to clear the debt.
fieldNote: His job looks safe here; the **pressure** is a thin cushion and **low pay** for his level.
He's rehearsed the **pay rise** conversation many times but hasn't had it yet.
He already uses AI **now and then** and sees the plateau as mildly helpful.

steps.text: Use the chat tool to draft routine letters to treasurers
Set up a standing order of a hundred a month into savings
Ask the partners for a raise using last year's billing figures

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one's closer to what the partners talk about at the away day. They've already bought a system that reads bank statements.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we should bring the tools in properly, with the staff in the room, not have them done to us. To friends I'd say the charity sector can't afford to lose the people who actually understand its accounts. Online I'd share stuff about the union campaign for fair AI rollouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my team of four probably becomes two, and I'd have to choose who stays, which is the part that keeps me awake. The checking and the reconciliations are exactly what these tools do. My job survives if I'm the one who runs the tools and talks to the treasurers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to pilot the new system with my team, once I'd seen it work at one other firm. I'd join the accountants' branch of the union and ask for a consultation. And I'd raise the savings to a hundred and fifty a month by cancelling the gym and the streaming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uncomfortable. Not panicked, but I'd feel responsible for four people's jobs, and I didn't sign up for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your four would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi, who's twenty-two and still in his exams. He's sharp but he hasn't got the client relationships yet. If they cut, the newest goes first, and I'd fight for him and probably lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the partners if they asked you to cut two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say give me six months to show the tools make us bigger, not smaller. Charities are crying out for proper accounts they can afford. If the tools make it cheaper, we take on more clients instead of losing people.

say: I'd say staff should be **in the room** when the firm brings tools in.
I'd share the union's campaign for **fair AI rollouts** in accounting firms.
think: Privately, my **team of four** probably becomes two, and I'd have to choose.
My job survives if I **run the tools** and keep talking to treasurers.
do: Pilot the new system with my team once it's **proven** at another firm.
Join the **union branch** and raise savings to **150 a month**.
feel: **Uncomfortable** and weighed down by being **responsible** for four people's jobs.
S1.quote: If the tools make charity accounts cheaper, we take on more clients instead of losing people.
fieldNote: His fear centres on **choosing** which colleagues go, more than losing his own role.
He's a classic **steady** adopter: he'll pilot, but only after seeing it work elsewhere.
His pitch to partners is to **grow** the client base rather than cut staff.

steps.text: Pilot the bank-reading system with his team after a visit elsewhere
Join the accountants' union branch and ask for consultation
Cancel the gym and streaming to save 150 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's frightening, to be honest. Two years is nothing. Our firm takes two years to agree on a new coffee machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs governments to step in now: a pause, or at least income support for people whose jobs vanish. At work I'd say we should be honest with clients and staff about what's coming. Online I'd be angry, and I'd probably say so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think I lose my job within a year of it arriving, because almost everything I do is thinking work at a screen. The robots coming later doesn't help me at all. Ruth's teaching might hold on a bit longer, because a classroom of seven-year-olds needs a person in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop paying into anything optional and keep every spare penny, maybe two hundred a month. I'd look at public sector finance jobs straight away, because they move slower. Ruth and I would shelve the plan to start trying for a baby next year, which is the hardest part to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Like standing on a platform and hearing the train you need is cancelled, with no replacement bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the baby. Is that really off the table?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not off the table, just pushed back. We'd want to know one of us has a job that'll last. If Ruth's job is the steady one, maybe I'm at home more, but on one teacher's salary with no savings, I don't see how.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look at public sector jobs. Would you also learn the AI properly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn enough to be useful in the transition, yes. But if it can do almost all thinking work in two years, being good at it buys me months, not a career. I'd rather spend the time somewhere with a union contract and slower rules.

say: I'd call for a **pause** or at least **income support** for people losing jobs.
I'd tell clients and staff **honestly** what's coming, and I'd be angry online.
think: Privately, I expect to **lose my job** within a year, as it's nearly all screen work.
My partner Ruth's **teaching** might last longer, because classrooms still need a person.
do: Cut every optional payment and save about **two hundred** a month.
Apply for **public sector** finance jobs right away and **delay** trying for a baby.
feel: **Scared**, like hearing his train is cancelled with **no replacement**.
S2.quote: Our firm takes two years to agree on a new coffee machine.
fieldNote: He expects to lose his job, and the **baby plan** is the first casualty he names.
He sees **Ruth's teaching** as the household's steadier income in this picture.
He'd learn AI only for the **transition**, believing it buys months, not a career.

steps.text: Cut optional spending and save two hundred a month
Apply for public sector finance jobs in the city
Delay trying for a baby until one job looks secure

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's long enough to do something, which somehow makes it feel worse if you then don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to set up proper support: retraining money, slower rollouts, protections for people mid-career. I'd push the union to get firms to agree on it now, not later. With friends I'd be more measured, but I'd still say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years lets me move sideways before it lands. I'd still lose the Calder Row job, but I could be somewhere sturdier by then. The charity sector itself might need someone who understands both the money and the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start using the AI tools every week, not now and then, and become the person at the firm who knows them. I'd apply for a finance manager job inside a big charity, because they'd need someone to oversee the tools. I'd save a hundred and fifty a month and keep the baby plan, just a year later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but with a handrail. I can see a route, even if it's narrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The owners who'd pocket the savings and the governments that let them. Not the software itself. It's a tool, and tools are only as fair as whoever decides who keeps the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Kofi, your junior?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to finish his exams and spend time with clients, not just spreadsheets. The relationship part might last longest. And I'd tell him to join the union, because nobody else will fight for him.

say: I'd say there are **five years** to fund retraining and **protect** mid-career workers.
I'd push the **union** to get firms to agree terms now.
think: Privately, five years lets me **move sideways** before the Calder Row job goes.
Charities might need someone who understands **money and tools** together.
do: Use AI tools **every week** and become the firm's go-to person for them.
Apply for a **finance manager** role at a large charity, and save **150 a month**.
feel: **Worried**, but holding a **handrail**: a narrow route he can see.
S3.quote: Tools are only as fair as whoever decides who keeps the money.
fieldNote: He blames **owners and government**, not the technology itself.
The extra time turns him from **steady** to actively learning, with the baby plan delayed a year.
His escape route stays inside the **charity sector** he cares about.

steps.text: Use AI tools weekly and become the firm's go-to person
Apply for a finance manager role at a large charity
Save 150 a month and delay the baby plan by a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven, maybe with a kid in school. That's a different life to plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this fairly if we start now: retraining paid by the firms that save, and shorter weeks instead of layoffs. I'd say it at union meetings and at Ruth's school fete if anyone asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd make it to forty with work, but not the same work. I'd probably be overseeing AI-done accounts for charities, or doing something with people, like grant advice. The firm as it is now won't exist in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Calder Row for a couple of years and learn the tools as they're proven. I'd start a part-time course in charity governance this year, which costs about six hundred. And Ruth and I would go ahead with trying for a baby, because ten years is a lifetime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but there's real hope in it. It feels like a long bend in the road rather than a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten years is a lifetime. What would you tell your future kid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them that their dad used to tick bank statements and then learned to do something else. I'd want them to see changing as normal. My own dad worked thirty years at the same depot, and I don't think that's coming back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the money worry go away with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the thin savings are still there. But ten years gives me time to build a cushion slowly, even a hundred a month adds up. I'd sleep better than in the other two.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough to do this fairly, with **shorter weeks** instead of layoffs.
I'd argue retraining should be **paid by firms** that save money from AI.
think: Privately, I'd still have work at forty, but **not the same work**.
Calder Row as it is now **won't exist** in ten years.
do: Stay at Calder Row and learn tools **as they're proven**.
Start a part-time **charity governance course** costing about **six hundred** this year.
feel: **Uneasy** but **hopeful**, like a long bend in the road rather than a cliff.
S4.quote: My own dad worked thirty years at the same depot, and I don't think that's coming back.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him go ahead with the **baby plan**, a clear marker of reduced fear.
He still expects to **lose this job**, but has time to move toward governance or grant advice.
He frames change as **normal** and wants his future child to see it that way.

steps.text: Start a part-time charity governance course costing about six hundred
Stay at Calder Row and learn tools once proven elsewhere
Go ahead with trying for a baby next year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it lands before we've got any savings or a plan. What would help is income support for people whose jobs go, at least a year of it, and funded retraining. And I'd want firms made to consult staff, through a union, before they cut.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about who gets the savings. If AI does my work, somebody's making more money. I'd like some of it to reach the staff, or the charities we serve, rather than just the partners.

headlineQuote: If AI does my work, somebody's making more money, and I'd like some of it to reach the staff.
portrait: Emeka is a **27-year-old** chartered accountant leading a team of four on **charity accounts** in an old mill city.
He lives with his partner Ruth, a teacher, with **less than a month** saved and a pay gap he resents.
He's a **steady** adopter who uses AI now and then and wants proof before going further.
His instincts are **collective**: union consultation, fair rollouts and income support.
He expects to lose his job under fast AGI and shelves a **baby**, but plans calmly with ten years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, because it arrives before they have **savings** or a plan.
whatWouldHelp: A year of **income support** and funded retraining for people whose jobs go.
Firms made to **consult staff** through a union before cutting.
